messages.author: 827384b6e9f2b83b
messages.subject: Help with high null model estimates
parts:
Hi All,

I used a stratified random sampling design. 5 regions (strata) with 9 randomly selected sampling sites within each region, for a total of 45 sampling sites. Each site was sampled for a 7 night period 4 times each year (corresponding to bat reproductive cycles) during the 3 year study. This provided 84 discrete observations for each of the 45 sampling sites (7x4x3 = 84).


I have 1121 instances of presence and 2529 instances of "absence" (a total of 3650 samples). There were 130 samples that I had to throw out because of power issues so I'm assuming those don't get factored in to the analysis. 

I’m more interested in occupancy estimates in the regions and habitat types as a whole rather than occupancy at the site level but currently the null model estimate of occupancy is high (possibly due to the high number of repeated sampling). Do I need to be concerned about this or do I need to pay more attention to the most general model? Here is my output below.

Hi Jim,
Thanks for you response. I'm still unclear as to whether or not the estimate for occupancy of 1 or 100% (or possibly 10, although I hope that's just the output squishing the 0 from the SE value 0.00423) is too high, or an indicator that something is wrong with the data. Although all sites had one detection, bats weren't detected every night at these sites. The backtransformed estimate of p appears to be .39 or 39% which seems reasonable but I want to make sure that I can use occupancy analysis on this data as it is, or if I will have to consider other options before I get too invested in  comparing AIC or QAIC values. 
Also, could you explain how you derived the estimates of occupancy for the 12 primary survey periods based off of the output? I was under the impression that the null model is showing parameter estimates over the entire study period and that this is the model I need to pay attention to before building the more complex models.         1 0.00423    8.38           1

Cheers,

messages.author: 01f32dcbb5507b45
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Help with high null model estimates
parts:
Hi Rachel,

If you detected bats at least once in all the surveyed sites each year, it implies that occupancy = 1. Therefore, there is no variation in your data that can be attributed to differences in the occurrence of the bats - all the variation will be due to differences between repeated surveys, not any underlying variability in occupancy. 

However, it is a different scenario if the levels of occupation varied yearly, did you detect bats in all sites every year? 

Cheers

Pablo

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Help with high null model estimates
parts:
Your model estimates 4 parameters:  psi1 (occupancy probability for year 1), g (colonization probability), e (extinction probability), and p (detection probability).  (Or rather colext directly estimates the logit of those parameters.)  Those estimates are

    psi1 = 1 - 1/(1 + exp (8.38)) = 0.9997706
    g = 1 - 1/(1 + exp(0.715)) = 0.671505
    e = 1 - 1/(1 + exp(-1.31)) = 0.2124868
    p = 1 - 1/(1 + exp (-0.433)) = 0.3934102
 
The occupancy probabilities for the remaining primary survey periods are

    psi2 = psi1*(1-e) + (1-psi1)*g = 0.787487
    psi3 = psi2*(1-e) + (1-psi2)*g = 0.76286
    psi4 = psi3*(1-e) + (1-psi3)*g = 0.760003
    .
    .
    .

There are functions in unmarked to get all of the above but I've just written the formulas to make it more explicit.

I'd be happy to look at the data if you want to send it offline.  (Maybe Pablo Garcia has the answer in that the first primary period had at least one detection at all sites?)


Jim

parts:
Hi Rachel,

I was talking about years because it is a commonly used temporal scale, but it doesn't need to be the one used in the study (only if it makes sense). You are correct, you should have a look at the detection history in each primary period. Still, you seem to have a very high occupancy rate, so it is likely that the variability in your data would be due to the imperfect detection. 

Note that if you have more than one primary period per year, then the estimates of the model will refer to the probabilities of extinction and colonisation for the periods spanned between primary periods. 

Cheers

Pablo
2017-08-24 5:46 GMT+12:00 Rachel Moseley <moseley...@gmail.com>:

Hi Pablo,
Thank you for your explanation. When you put it that way it does make sense that occupancy would be 1 by looking at the null model. I did detect bats at least once in all sites in year 1 and year 3, but only detected bats in 44 of the 45 sites in year 2. Are you asking if occupation varied yearly in the true sense of the word "year" or should I be looking at detections in each primary survey period (in my case they are different). I have 12 primary survey periods and 3 years. 
Cheers,
Rachel


On Tuesday, August 22, 2017 at 4:09:40 PM UTC-10, Pablo García wrote:
Hi Rachel,

If you detected bats at least once in all the surveyed sites each year, it implies that occupancy = 1. Therefore, there is no variation in your data that can be attributed to differences in the occurrence of the bats - all the variation will be due to differences between repeated surveys, not any underlying variability in occupancy. 

However, it is a different scenario if the levels of occupation varied yearly, did you detect bats in all sites every year? 

Cheers

Pablo
